Homarus gammarus , known as the European lobster or common lobster , is a species of clawed lobster from the eastern Atlantic Ocean , Mediterranean Sea and parts of the Black Sea . It is closely related to the American lobster , H. americanus . It may grow to a length of 60 cm ( 24 in ) and a mass of 6 kilograms ( 13 lb ) , and bears a conspicuous pair of claws . In life , the lobsters are blue , only becoming " lobster red " on cooking . Mating occurs in the summer , producing eggs which are carried by the females for up to a year before hatching into planktonic larvae . Homarus gammarus is a highly esteemed food , and is widely caught using lobster pots , mostly around the British Isles . 
 Homarus gammarus is a large crustacean , with a body length up to 60 centimetres ( 24 in ) and weighing up to 5 – 6 kilograms ( 11 – 13 lb ) , although the lobsters caught in lobster pots are usually 23 – 38 cm ( 9 – 15 in ) long and weigh 0 @.@ 7 – 2 @.@ 2 kg ( 1 @.@ 5 – 4 @.@ 9 lb ) . Like other crustaceans , lobsters have a hard exoskeleton which they must shed in order to grow , in a process called ecdysis ( moulting ) . This may occur several times a year for young lobsters , but decreases to once every 1 – 2 years for larger animals . 
 The first pair of pereiopods is armed with a large , asymmetrical pair of claws . The larger one is the " crusher " , and has rounded nodules used for crushing prey ; the other is the " cutter " , which has sharp inner edges , and is used for holding or tearing the prey . Usually , the left claw is the crusher , and the right is the cutter . 
 The exoskeleton is generally blue above , with spots that coalesce , and yellow below . The red colour associated with lobsters only appears after cooking . This occurs because , in life , the red pigment astaxanthin is bound to a protein complex , but the complex is broken up by the heat of cooking , releasing the red pigment . 
 The closest relative of H. gammarus is the American lobster , Homarus americanus . The two species are very similar , and can be crossed artificially , although hybrids are unlikely to occur in the wild since their ranges do not overlap .  Female H. gammarus reach sexual maturity when they have grown to a carapace length of 80 – 85 millimetres ( 3 @.@ 1 – 3 @.@ 3 in ) , whereas males mature at a slightly smaller size . Mating typically occurs in summer between a recently moulted female , whose shell is therefore soft , and a hard @-@ shelled male . The female carries the eggs for up to 12 months , depending on the temperature , attached to her pleopods . Females carrying eggs are said to be " berried " and can be found throughout the year . 
 The eggs hatch at night , and the larvae swim to the water surface where they drift with the ocean currents , preying on zooplankton . This stage involves three moults and lasts for 15 – 35 days . After the third moult , the juvenile takes on a form closer to the adult , and adopts a benthic lifestyle . The juveniles are rarely seen in the wild , and are poorly known , although they are known to be capable of digging extensive burrows . It is estimated that only 1 larva in every 20 @,@ 000 survives to the benthic phase . When they reach a carapace length of 15 mm ( 0 @.@ 59 in ) , the juveniles leave their burrows and start their adult lives .

It is also present in most of the Mediterranean Sea , only missing from the section east of Crete , and along only the north @-@ west coast of the Black Sea .  The species can be divided into four genetically distinct populations , one widespread population , and three which have diverged due to small effective population sizes , possibly due to adaptation to the local environment . The first of these is the population of lobsters from northern Norway , which have been referred to as the " midnight @-@ sun lobster " . The populations in the Mediterranean Sea are distinct from those in the Atlantic Ocean . The last distinct population is found in the Netherlands : samples from the <unk> were distinct from those collected in the North Sea or English Channel . 
 Attempts have been made to introduce H. gammarus to New Zealand , alongside other European species such as the edible crab , Cancer pagurus . Between 1904 and 1914 , one million lobster larvae were released from hatcheries in Dunedin , but the species did not become established there . 
 Adult H. gammarus live on the continental shelf at depths of 0 – 150 metres ( 0 – 492 ft ) , although not normally deeper than 50 m ( 160 ft ) . They prefer hard substrates , such as rocks or hard mud , and live in holes or crevices , emerging at night to feed .

 Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam , CB , CBE ( 15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976 ) was a senior commander in the Royal Australian Air Force ( RAAF ) . Born and educated in Tasmania , he joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934 . He specialised in flying instruction and navigation before the outbreak of World War II . In April 1941 , he became commanding officer of No. 2 Squadron , which operated Lockheed Hudsons . The squadron was deployed to Dutch Timor in December , and saw action against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific . After returning to Australia in February 1942 , Headlam held staff appointments and training commands , finishing the war a group captain . 
 Headlam served as Officer Commanding North @-@ Western Area in 1946 , and as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950 . In 1950 – 51 , during the Malayan Emergency , he was stationed at Singapore as commander of No. 90 ( Composite ) Wing and , later , RAF Tengah . He twice served as acting Air Member for Personnel , in 1957 and 1959 – 60 , receiving appointment as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958 . Promoted air vice marshal , he successively held the positions of Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) Operational Command in 1961 – 62 , AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia – Malaysia Konfrontasi , Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965 – 66 , and AOC Support Command in 1966 – 67 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965 . Following a posting to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff from 1968 to 1971 , he retired from the Air Force and died in Melbourne five years later . 
 The son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam , Frank Headlam was born on 15 July 1914 in Launceston , Tasmania . He was schooled at <unk> College , Hobart , and matriculated in 1932 . He underwent flying instruction with No. 1 Flying Training School ( FTS ) at RAAF Point Cook , Victoria , and was commissioned as a pilot officer on 1 January 1935 .

No larger than a flight according to the official history of the pre @-@ war RAAF , Seaplane Squadron was part of No. 1 FTS and operated Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes , among other types . During this posting Headlam was promoted to flying officer , on 1 July 1935 , and wrote a paper on national defence in which he suggested that with " strong air forces , naval forces ( including submarines ) , and fixed defences , Australia may be made practically invulnerable " . According to Air Force historian Alan Stephens , this paper " in effect , defined the ' anti @-@ lodgment ' concept which has been a persistent feature of RAAF strategic thinking " . 
 Headlam completed a flying instructors course in July 1936 and joined the staff of No. 1 FTS . He was promoted to flight lieutenant on 1 March 1937 . Commencing in July 1938 , he was one of six students to take part in the RAAF 's first Long Specialist Navigation Course , run by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook . The course involved several epic training flights that attracted considerable media attention , including a twelve @-@ day , 10 @,@ 800 @-@ kilometre ( 6 @,@ 700 mi ) round @-@ Australia trip by three Avro Ansons , one of which was piloted by Headlam , in November . The following month , Headlam led the three Ansons on a six @-@ day journey back and forth over Central Australia . He subsequently passed the navigation course with a special distinction . On 27 January 1939 he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton , Victoria , as a flight commander . He served initially with No. 2 Squadron , before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on 29 August . Both units operated Ansons . 
 Following the outbreak of World War II , No. 1 Squadron was engaged in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance duties off south @-@ eastern Australia . Headlam continued to serve with the squadron as a flight commander until 15 January 1940 , when he was assigned to Headquarters Laverton as the station navigation officer . On 27 March he was posted to the staff of RAAF Headquarters , Melbourne . He was promoted to squadron leader on 1 June 1940 . Two weeks later he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul 's Anglican Church in Frankston ; the couple would have a son and a daughter . 
 Headlam was given command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on 15 April 1941 , and raised to wing commander on 1 July . Equipped with Lockheed Hudsons , the squadron mainly conducted maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December , when four of its aircraft were ordered to Darwin , Northern Territory , in response to fears of Japanese aggression in the Pacific . On 7 December , this detachment established itself at Penfui , near Koepang in Dutch Timor , while No. 2 Squadron 's eight remaining Hudsons were stationed at Darwin on standby . The following day , aware that Australia was now at war in the Pacific , one of the Penfui @-@ based Hudsons attacked the Japanese <unk> Nanyo Maru , which was suspected of being a radio ship , and forced it aground . By 12 December , Headlam had transferred to Penfui as commanding officer of the base , as well as No. 2 Squadron .

Eastern Area Command , considered a de facto operational headquarters owing to the preponderance of combat units under its control , was reorganised as Home Command in October 1953 . He was promoted to acting air commodore in May . His appointment as aide @-@ de @-@ camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced on 7 October 1954 . 
 Headlam was promoted to substantive air commodore on 1 January 1955 . In November he was posted to RAAF Overseas Headquarters , London , and the following year undertook studies at the Imperial Defence College . Returning to Australia , he served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air , Canberra , from 19 March to 21 October 1957 , between the terms of Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters , and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960 , between the terms of Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely . In this role Headlam occupied a seat on the Air Board , the service 's controlling body that comprised its senior officers and was chaired by the Chief of the Air Staff . He was also one of two RAAF representatives to serve on a committee , chaired by businessman William John Allison , examining conditions of defence service ; the committee 's recommendations led to a doubling of flight pay , among other improvements . Headlam 's other positions at the Department of Air included Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959 , and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959 . The latter assignment put him in charge of the RAAF 's Directorate of Intelligence . Headlam was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire ( CBE ) in the 1958 Queen 's Birthday Honours , gazetted on 3 June . In May 1960 he became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff . 
 On 30 January 1961 , Headlam joined the staff of Operational Command ( OPCOM ) , the successor organisation to Home Command , responsible for the direction of RAAF operational units . He took over as Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) OPCOM from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock in April . Headlam was promoted to air vice marshal on 29 May . On 17 July 1962 , he was posted to RAAF Base Butterworth , Malaya , and took up the appointment of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore one week later . He was succeeded as AOC OPCOM by Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch . As AOC No. 224 Group , Headlam had overall responsibility for regional air defence and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 , and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia that officially began the following month . Divorced from his first wife in 1956 , he married widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on 20 January 1964 . He handed over No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley @-@ Norris on 30 November . 
 Returning to Australia , Headlam became Deputy Chief of the Air Staff ( DCAS ) on 26 January 1965 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath ( CB ) " in recognition of distinguished service in the Borneo Territories " on 22 June . His tenure as DCAS coincided with the most significant rearmament program the Air Force had undertaken since World War II , and with manpower shortages stemming from this expansion and from Australia 's increasing involvement in the security of South East Asia . The first RAAF helicopters were committed to the Vietnam War towards the end of his term , and he travelled to Saigon with the Chief of the General Staff , Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton , in March 1966 to plan the deployment . The year before , Wilton had recommended to Air Marshal Murdoch , the Chief of the Air Staff , that two Iroquois be sent to Vietnam for familiarisation purposes ; Murdoch had rebuffed Wilton , and the RAAF helicopter squadron was considered underprepared for its army co @-@ operation role when it finally did deploy . On 1 January 1968 , Headlam was posted to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff . He served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971 . 
 Returning to Australia in June 1971 , Headlam took resettlement leave before retiring from the Air Force on 3 August . He made his home in Melbourne , where he died aged 62 on 23 December 1976 , after a lengthy battle with cancer . Survived by his children and his second wife , he was given a private funeral and cremated at Springvale Crematorium .

 The current M @-@ 82 dates back to 1926 . It ran from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M @-@ 46 in Howard City . Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam, CB, CBE (15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976) served as a high-ranking officer in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF). A native of Tasmania where he completed his education, Headlam entered the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934. Prior to World War II, he developed expertise in navigation and flight instruction. Taking command of No. 2 Squadron in April 1941, he led operations with Lockheed Hudson aircraft. His squadron was stationed in Dutch Timor in December and engaged in combat operations against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific theater. Following his return to Australia in February 1942, Headlam took on various staff and training leadership roles, and by war's end had attained the rank of group captain.

Headlam's military career included several significant appointments, beginning with his role as Officer Commanding North-Western Area in 1946, followed by his position as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950. During the Malayan Emergency (1950-51), he commanded No. 90 (Composite) Wing in Singapore before taking charge of RAF Tengah. He temporarily served as Air Member for Personnel twice, in 1957 and 1959-60, and was honored as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958. After his promotion to air vice marshal, he held various high-ranking positions: Air Officer Commanding (AOC) Operational Command (1961-62), AOC No. 224 Group RAF during the Indonesia-Malaysia Konfrontasi (1962-65), Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (1965-66), and AOC Support Command (1966-67). In 1965, he was recognized as a Companion of the Order of the Bath. His final posting was in London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff (1968-71), after which he retired from the Air Force. He passed away in Melbourne five years after his retirement.

Frank Headlam, born in Launceston, Tasmania on July 15, 1914, was raised by his farming parents, Malcolm and Hilda Headlam. After completing his education at College in Hobart and graduating in 1932, he made the bold decision to enlist in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) as an air cadet on January 16, 1934, despite his parents' disapproval. He received his flight training at No. 1 Flying Training School (FTS) at RAAF Point Cook, Victoria, and achieved the rank of pilot officer on January 1, 1935.

Following his conversion course completion, Headlam joined the Seaplane Squadron stationed at Point Cook. The squadron, which was a subunit of No. 1 FTS and no bigger than a flight according to pre-war RAAF records, operated various aircraft including Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes. While serving there, Headlam received a promotion to flying officer on July 1, 1935, and authored a significant paper on national defense. In this paper, he proposed that Australia could achieve near-invulnerability through a combination of "strong air forces, naval forces (including submarines), and fixed defenses." Air Force historian Alan Stephens later noted that this paper effectively established the 'anti-lodgment' concept, which would become a lasting element in RAAF strategic thinking.

Headlam joined the staff of No. 1 FTS after completing his flying instructors course in July 1936, and received promotion to flight lieutenant on March 1, 1937. In July 1938, he was selected as one of six participants in the RAAF's inaugural Long Specialist Navigation Course at Point Cook, under the instruction of Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch. The course featured several notable training expeditions that garnered significant press coverage, including a remarkable November journey where Headlam piloted one of three Avro Ansons on a 10,800-kilometer (6,700-mile) circumnavigation of Australia lasting twelve days. In December, he led the three Ansons on another significant mission, conducting a six-day expedition across Central Australia. His exceptional performance earned him a special distinction upon completing the navigation course. Following this achievement, he was assigned to RAAF Station Laverton, Victoria, as a flight commander on January 27, 1939, initially serving with No. 2 Squadron before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on August 29, with both units utilizing Anson aircraft.

After World War II began, No. 1 Squadron conducted maritime patrol operations, protecting convoys and performing reconnaissance along Australia's southeastern coast. Serving as a flight commander, Headlam remained with the squadron until January 15, 1940, when he took up the position of station navigation officer at Headquarters Laverton. He then transferred to RAAF Headquarters in Melbourne on March 27. Headlam attained the rank of squadron leader on June 1, 1940. Shortly after, on June 15, he wed Katherine Bridge in a ceremony at St Paul's Anglican Church, Frankston, and they later became parents to two children - a boy and a girl.

Headlam assumed leadership of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on April 15, 1941, and was promoted to wing commander on July 1. The squadron, operating Lockheed Hudson aircraft, primarily conducted maritime surveillance in southern regions until December 5, when four aircraft were dispatched to Darwin, Northern Territory, due to growing concerns about Japanese aggression in the Pacific. The detachment established a base at Penfui, near Koepang in Dutch Timor, on December 7, while the squadron's remaining eight Hudsons were positioned on alert in Darwin. The next day, following Australia's entry into the Pacific War, one of the Penfui-based Hudsons engaged the Japanese vessel Nanyo Maru, suspected of being a communications ship, forcing it to run aground. By December 12, Headlam had relocated to Penfui, where he served as both base commander and leader of No. 2 Squadron.

In January 1942, No. 2 Squadron had its aircraft distributed across three locations: Penfui, <unk> Island, and Darwin. The unit's detachment at Penfui engaged Japanese vessels involved in the Celebes invasion. On January 11, two Hudson aircraft managed to shoot down or damage three Japanese floatplanes while bombing a transport vessel, though both Hudsons were subsequently destroyed by Mitsubishi Zeros the following day. Japanese forces began regular bombing raids on Penfui starting January 26, 1942, causing damage to several aircraft. While the operational Hudsons were evacuated to Darwin, Headlam and his personnel remained at Penfui to maintain the base for Australian reconnaissance missions. Following orders on February 18, Headlam evacuated most personnel, leaving a small team with Sparrow Force to destroy the airfield. Upon his return to Darwin the next day, the city experienced its first Japanese raid, resulting in the destruction of four No. 2 Squadron Hudsons. The surviving aircraft were moved to Daly Waters, from where they continued reconnaissance and bombing operations against Japanese positions in Timor.

Headlam served as Controller of Operations at North-Western Area Command Headquarters in Darwin until May 12, 1942, before transferring to Victoria to command No. 2 Air Navigation School in Nhill, where they operated Anson aircraft. In June, No. 97 (Reserve) Squadron was established using the school's personnel. He later assumed command of No. 2 Air Observer School at Mount Gambier, South Australia, on July 20, 1943, which also utilized Ansons. Following his promotion to group captain on December 1, 1943, he became the first commanding officer of No. 3 unit at Port Pirie on December 9, overseeing operations of both Ansons and Fairey Battles. After relinquishing this command, he began his studies at RAAF Staff School in Mount Martha, Victoria, on October 2, 1944. His final posting came on January 12, 1945, when he took the position of senior administrative staff officer at North-Western Area Command.

In January 1946, Headlam assumed the role of Officer Commanding North-Western Area. Later that year, he relocated to Britain, where he enrolled at the Royal Air Force Staff College in Andover and worked with RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London. Following his return to Australia in November 1947, he took up the position of Director of Training at RAAF Headquarters. By November 1950, he succeeded Group Captain Paddy Heffernan as commander of No. 90 (Composite) Wing, based at RAF Changi, Singapore. Under his command, the wing oversaw RAAF operations during the Malayan Emergency, coordinating No. 1 (Bomber) Squadron's Avro Lincolns and No. 38 (Transport) Squadron's Douglas C-47 Dakotas. The Lincoln aircraft conducted both widespread bombing campaigns and precision strikes in communist-controlled regions, while the Dakotas performed various missions including courier services, VIP transportation, medical evacuations throughout South East Asia, and in Malaya specifically, they handled troop transport, supply drops, and propaganda leaflet distribution. On December 20, Headlam sustained minor injuries when a No. 38 Squadron Dakota he was co-piloting crashed at Kampong Aur in Pahang after experiencing engine problems during a supply drop mission. His responsibilities expanded in August 1951 when he was appointed commander of RAF Tengah, Singapore, while maintaining his position as commanding officer of No. 90 Wing. His tenure as commander of No. 90 Wing concluded in December 1951.

On February 19, 1952, Headlam assumed the position of senior air staff officer (SASO) at Eastern Area Command, located in Penrith, New South Wales. During his tenure as SASO, the RAAF modernized its fleet with the introduction of English Electric Canberra jet bombers and CAC Sabre jet fighters. The Air Force underwent a significant structural reorganization during this period, shifting from a geographic-based command and control structure to a functional one, which led to the creation of Home (operational), Training, and Maintenance Commands. In October 1953, Eastern Area Command, which had effectively served as an operational headquarters due to its extensive control over combat units, was transformed into Home Command. In recognition of his "exceptional ability and devotion to duty," Headlam was honored as an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 1954 New Year Honours. He was promoted to acting air commodore in May, and on October 7, 1954, he was appointed as aide-de-camp to Queen Elizabeth II.

Headlam achieved the permanent rank of air commodore on January 1, 1955. He was subsequently assigned to RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London that November, followed by academic pursuits at the Imperial Defence College the next year. Back in Australia, he took on the role of acting Air Member for Personnel at Canberra's Department of Air twice: first from March 19 to October 21, 1957, bridging the gap between Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters, and again from August 24, 1959, to March 28, 1960, between Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely. This position granted him membership on the Air Board, the service's governing body of senior officers led by the Chief of the Air Staff. He also served as one of two RAAF delegates on a committee headed by businessman William John Allison, which reviewed defence service conditions and achieved significant improvements, including a 100% increase in flight pay. At the Department of Air, Headlam also served as Air Commodore Plans (October 1957 to January 1959) and Director General Plans and Policy (January to August 1959), with the latter role placing him in charge of the RAAF's Directorate of Intelligence. He was honored as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in the Queen's Birthday Honours, officially announced on June 3, 1958. By May 1960, he had advanced to the position of acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff.

On January 30, 1961, Headlam began his role at Operational Command (OPCOM), which had replaced Home Command as the organization overseeing RAAF operational units. He succeeded Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock as Air Officer Commanding (AOC) OPCOM in April. His promotion to air vice marshal followed on May 29. Headlam's subsequent assignment took him to RAAF Base Butterworth in Malaya on July 17, 1962, where he assumed command of No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore a week later, with Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch taking his place as AOC OPCOM. In his position as AOC No. 224 Group, Headlam oversaw regional air defense and offensive air operations during both the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 and the ensuing Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia, which formally began the following month. After divorcing his first wife in 1956, he wed Vernon Spence, a widowed social worker, at Sydney's registry office on January 20, 1964. His command of No. 224 Group concluded on November 30, when he transferred leadership to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley-Norris.

Upon his return to Australia, Headlam assumed the role of Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (DCAS) on January 26, 1965. He received recognition as a Companion of the Order of the Bath (CB) on June 22 for his distinguished service in the Borneo Territories. His DCAS period coincided with the Air Force's largest rearmament initiative since World War II, while facing personnel challenges due to this expansion and Australia's growing involvement in South East Asian security. During the final phase of his term, the RAAF initiated its helicopter deployment to the Vietnam War, and he accompanied Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton, the Chief of the General Staff, to Saigon in March 1966 to coordinate the deployment plans. The previous year, Wilton had suggested to Air Marshal Murdoch, the Chief of the Air Staff, that two Iroquois helicopters be deployed to Vietnam for familiarization purposes. However, Murdoch rejected this proposal, which ultimately led to the RAAF helicopter squadron being inadequately prepared for its army cooperation duties upon deployment. On August 8, 1966, Headlam took over from Air Vice Marshal Douglas Candy as AOC of Support Command in Melbourne, an organization established in 1959 through the merger of the RAAF's Training and Maintenance Commands. He was later appointed as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff in London on January 1, 1968, and served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from November 17, 1970, until June 5, 1971.

After coming back to Australia in June 1971, Headlam spent time on resettlement leave until his formal retirement from the Air Force on August 3rd. He settled in Melbourne, where he passed away at age 62 on December 23, 1976, following an extended struggle with cancer. His second wife and children outlived him, and he received a private funeral service followed by cremation at Springvale Crematorium.

M-82 is a Michigan state highway located in the Lower Peninsula, connecting the cities of Fremont and Howard City. Running through Fremont and bordering the southern part of Manistee National Forest between Newaygo and Howard City, this road represents the second iteration of the M-82 designation. The first M-82 was established in the Upper Peninsula around 1919, while the current Lower Peninsula route dates back to the 1920s. Throughout its history, the western endpoint has varied, at times extending to New Era or Hesperia, before being finalized to its present configuration in the late 1970s.

M-82 originates at an intersection with M-120 and B-96 near Fremont, where three county boundaries meet. At this tripoint, M-120 serves as the boundary between Newaygo-Oceana and Newaygo-Muskegon counties, while B-96 marks the Oceana-Muskegon county line extending westward. From this intersection, M-82 heads east along 48th Street through agricultural areas into Fremont. Within the town, the route becomes Main Street through the downtown district before turning south onto Stewart Avenue. After a curve, it transforms into 72nd Street, continuing east through farmland. Approaching Newaygo, the landscape transitions to woodland near the Muskegon River. The highway follows Fremont Street eastward until meeting M-37, where both routes merge and cross the river along State Street into downtown. South of Newaygo's center, M-82 splits from M-37 and continues east along 82nd Street, skirting the southern boundary of the Manistee National Forest. The route terminates at exit 118 on US 131/M-46 west of Howard City.

The Michigan Department of Transportation (MDOT) monitors traffic volumes on its highway network as part of its ongoing maintenance duties. Traffic levels are measured using average annual daily traffic (AADT), a metric that calculates the typical daily vehicle count on a road segment throughout the year. According to the department's 2009 data, the busiest section of M-82 was located west of Fremont, recording 16,532 vehicles per day, while the lowest traffic count was observed east of Newaygo, with 4,018 vehicles daily. Furthermore, no portion of M-82 has been incorporated into the National Highway System, which consists of roads deemed crucial for the nation's economic strength, defense capabilities, and mobility needs.

The origins of M-82 can be traced to 1926, when it was established as a route connecting Hart's US 31 to Howard City's northern intersection of US 131 and M-46. The route passed through the communities of Ferry, Hesperia, and Fremont, taking over what was previously designated as M-41. A significant change occurred in late 1936 when M-46 was extended to include the segment between Newaygo and Howard City, creating a shared M-46/M-82 route to complete M-46's path. By 1938, this concurrent section was redesignated solely as M-46, which resulted in M-82 being shortened to terminate at the northern M-37 junction in Newaygo. Around the transition from 1947 to 1948, the highway underwent another modification when its western portion was realigned. Rather than maintaining its northwestern trajectory to Hart, the route was redirected westward to terminate in Shelby.

The highway underwent two western realignments in 1963 and 1964, establishing a new route from Hesperia to New Era that avoided Ferry. A significant reorganization of highway designations in Oceana County occurred around 1969: M-20 took over M-82's western segment from Hesperia to New Era, replacing its previous terminus at Muskegon. The newly designated M-120 replaced M-20 south of Hesperia, while M-82 was reduced to only cover the Hesperia-Newaygo section. In 1973, the highway's length expanded when its eastern terminus returned to Howard City. This change occurred as M-46 was redirected along the US 131 freeway from Howard City to Cedar Springs, then assumed M-57's route between Cedar Springs and Casnovia. This allowed M-82 to reclaim the Newaygo-Howard City stretch. The final modification came in 1978 when the shared section with M-120 was designated solely as M-120, and M-82 was shortened to end at the junction west of Fremont, creating its present-day configuration.

Shikamaru Nara is a fictional character created by Masashi Kishimoto for the Naruto manga and anime franchise. Within the series, he serves as a ninja in the village of Konohagakure and operates as part of Team 10, alongside teammates Choji Akimichi and Ino Yamanaka, under the leadership of Asuma Sarutobi. Despite possessing exceptional intelligence, Shikamaru is characterized by his laid-back demeanor and reluctance to exert himself, traits that have endeared him to his creator Kishimoto. Beyond the main manga and anime series, the character has made appearances in four Naruto feature films and has been featured in various franchise media, including video games and original video animations (OVAs).

Critics from various anime and manga publications have offered their perspectives on Shikamaru's character development. Reviewers frequently highlighted the contrast between his lazy demeanor and sharp intellect, while acknowledging his growth into a leadership role. The Anime News Network particularly praised how Shikamaru evolved into an "unexpected hero" within the Naruto series. The character has consistently ranked well in fan popularity polls among Naruto readers. Various Shikamaru-themed merchandise has been produced, including collectible action figures, key chains, and decorative patches.

Manga creator Masashi Kishimoto expressed his fondness for Shikamaru's character, particularly appreciating how the genius character maintains a laid-back demeanor, which he contrasted with Sasuke Uchiha's sharp intellect but harsh personality. In a humorous comment, Kishimoto stated that if he were female, he would choose to marry Shikamaru, believing in the character's potential for future success. When updating Shikamaru's appearance for Part II of the series, Kishimoto faced the challenge of making him stand out while still wearing the standard ninja vest. His solution was to place the forehead protector on Shikamaru's arm, allowing his distinctive hairstyle to remain visible.

Shikamaru makes his first significant appearance during the Chunin Exams, a biannual testing event where ninjas seek to advance their rank. As a member of Team 10, he works alongside his teammates Choji Akimichi and Ino Yamanaka. Despite possessing exceptional intelligence, with an IQ over 200 as assessed by his mentor Asuma Sarutobi, Shikamaru displays a notably lackadaisical attitude and strives to exert minimal effort in his daily life. His combat prowess centers around the Shadow Imitation Technique (Kagemane no Jutsu, known as "Shadow Possession Jutsu" in English broadcasts), his clan's trademark ability that allows him to merge his shadow with an opponent's, forcing them to mirror his movements while rendering them immobile. Throughout the series, his shadow manipulation skills evolve significantly. By Part II, Shikamaru demonstrates mastery over multiple shadow-based techniques simultaneously and can elevate his shadow off the ground to interact with physical objects, enabling him to attack enemies with shadow tendrils or launch weapons.

During the exams, Shikamaru displays characteristic indifference; although he successfully outmaneuvers the Sand Village ninja Temari, he chooses to surrender the match citing depleted chakra reserves. Nevertheless, his tactical brilliance and strategic thinking during the fight with Temari so impresses the exam evaluators that he becomes the sole candidate among his peers to achieve Chunin status. Following his promotion, Shikamaru leads a mission to stop Sasuke Uchiha's defection to the Sound Village. While his team successfully overcomes the Sound Village ninja blocking their path, they ultimately fail to prevent Sasuke's escape.

In the second part of the series, Shikamaru leads a mission to track down two Akatsuki organization members. Although his team successfully locates their targets, his mentor Asuma Sarutobi falls in battle to the immortal Akatsuki member Hidan, despite Shikamaru's valiant efforts. Following Asuma's memorial service, Shikamaru, accompanied by the remaining Team 10 members and Kakashi Hatake, embarks on a revenge mission. While his companions engage Hidan's partner Kakuzu, Shikamaru successfully avenges his mentor by defeating Hidan and ensuring his body remains permanently hidden. Afterward, Shikamaru pledges to protect both Kurenai Yuhi and her unborn child with Asuma. He later serves as a proxy general under Gaara in the Fourth Division, working alongside Temari and Choji. In the series' conclusion, fulfilling his aspirations from the final battles, Shikamaru becomes the Seventh Hokage Naruto's advisor, having married Temari and fathered a son named Shikadai Nara.

Throughout the Naruto franchise, Shikamaru appears in seven feature films, each showcasing different aspects of his character. In the second film, he supports Naruto Uzumaki and Sakura Haruno in their conflict with Haido, who seeks world domination through a mysterious power. The fourth film briefly shows him battling stone soldiers, while in the fifth, he joins Kakashi and Sai on a mission to locate the Land of Sky's headquarters before their planned invasion of Konoha. The sixth film features him fighting alongside Sakura and Sai against Hiruko's chimera beast, and in the eighth, he confronts the demon Satori. The ninth film presents an alternate universe where a heavyset Shikamaru contrasts with his teammate who assumes the strategic role, while the tenth film sees him leading a rescue team including Naruto, Sakura, Sai, and Hinata Hyuga to save Hanabi from Otsutsuki. Additionally, he makes an appearance in the third original video animation, participating in a tournament. Shikamaru is available as a playable character in virtually all Naruto video games, including both the Clash of Ninja and Ultimate Ninja series, where he sometimes employs Shadow Imitation Technique variants not seen in the original anime or manga. His first video game appearance in his Part II design was in Naruto Shippūden: Gekitō Ninja Taisen! EX 2.

A novel called Shikamaru Hiden: A Cloud Drifting in Silent Darkness features Shikamaru as both protagonist and narrator, with text by Takashi Yano and illustrations from Kishimoto. Taking place two years after the Fourth Ninja War, the story follows Shikamaru in his role coordinating the newly established Shinobi Union. His mission involves tracking down a rebel ninja who controls the faraway Land of Silence and seeks to create a new society governed by ordinary citizens. The narrative also delves into his deepening bond with Temari, concluding with a scene years later where he faces difficulty choosing a name for their child together.

Shikamaru has consistently demonstrated strong popularity in Weekly Shōnen Jump's polls for the series, maintaining a position within the top ten and once achieving fourth place. In the final poll conducted in 2011, he secured ninth position, placing between Sasori above and Hinata below. Various merchandise featuring Shikamaru has been produced, including action figures, key chains, and patches depicting both his Part I and Part II appearances. In a survey among NTT customers, he was selected as the sixteenth most popular black-haired male character in anime. Additionally, CyberConnect2's CEO Hiroshi Matsuyama has expressed that Shikamaru ranks among his favorite Naruto characters.

Various media critics and publications have offered their perspectives on Shikamaru's character in manga, anime, video games, and related content. Meridian ranks as Mississippi's sixth most populous city and serves as the seat of government for Lauderdale County in the United States. The city functions as the main urban center of the Meridian, Mississippi Micropolitan Statistical Area. Situated along major transportation routes, Meridian is positioned 93 miles (150 km) to the east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 km) to the west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 km) to the northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; and 231 miles (372 km) to the southeast of Memphis, Tennessee.

Meridian emerged in 1860 where the Mobile and Ohio Railroad met the Southern Railway of Mississippi, developing into a vital commercial hub due to its railroad-based economy and transportation network. The city's significance made it a target during the American Civil War, leading to its widespread destruction by Union General William Tecumseh Sherman's forces during the Battle of Meridian in February 1864.

Following post-war reconstruction, the city experienced a "Golden Age," becoming Mississippi's largest urban center from 1890 to 1930 and emerging as a prominent Southern manufacturing hub, with 44 daily train arrivals and departures. Union Station, constructed in 1906, now serves as a multi-modal transportation center that connects the Meridian Transit System, Greyhound Buses, and Trailways, serving approximately 242,360 passengers annually. While the city's economy slowed as the railroad industry declined, it has successfully diversified, with healthcare, military, and manufacturing sectors becoming the primary employers as of 2010. According to 2008 census data, the city proper has 38,232 residents, but its economic influence extends to a population of 232,900 within a 45-mile (72 km) radius and 526,500 within a 65-mile (105 km) radius, with respective labor forces of 104,600 and 234,200 people supporting the local economy.

The region's economy is significantly supported by two key military installations: Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, jointly providing employment for more than 4,000 individuals. NAS Meridian hosts both the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy (RCTA) and Mississippi's first Department of Homeland Security facility. Key Field, which earned its name from the Key brothers, Fred and Al, who achieved a world flight endurance record in 1935, currently serves as the base for two military units: the Air National Guard's 186th Air Refueling Wing and the Army National Guard's 185th Aviation Brigade support facility. In the non-military sector, Rush Foundation Hospital stands as the area's largest employer, with a workforce of 2,610 people.

The city boasts a rich cultural landscape featuring several prominent institutions, including the Riley Center, the Meridian Museum of Art, Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. During the segregation period, Meridian hosted two Carnegie libraries – one serving the white community and another serving African Americans. The Carnegie Branch Library, which served the African American community and was among several such libraries built in the South during segregation, has since been demolished.

Meridian has been chosen to host the future Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center. The city proudly claims Jimmie Rodgers, widely known as the "Father of Country Music," as one of its native sons. In Highland Park, visitors can explore a museum featuring Rodgers' memorabilia and historic steam locomotive artifacts. The park's crown jewel is the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel, distinguished as a National Historic Landmark and recognized as the world's last remaining two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie. The city has produced several other prominent figures, including Susan Akin, who won Miss America 1986; civil rights activist James Chaney, who tragically lost his life in the 1964 Mississippi civil rights workers murders; and Hartley Peavey, who established the Meridian-based Peavey Electronics. The city's federal courthouse made history during 1966-1967 when it hosted a landmark trial concerning Chaney's murder and that of two fellow activists, marking the first instance where a white jury found a white official guilty in a civil rights killing.

The territory that is now Meridian was originally home to the Choctaw Native Americans before being acquired by the United States through the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek during the Indian Removal period in 1830. Following the treaty's ratification, settlers of European-American descent began populating the region.

After acquiring a federal land grant of approximately 2,000 acres (810 ha), Meridian's first settler, Richard McLemore, initiated a strategy of offering free land to newcomers to promote settlement and development in the area. In 1853, the majority of McLemore's property was purchased by Lewis A. Ragsdale, an Alabama attorney, while the remaining 80 acres (0.32 km2) were acquired by John T. Ball, a merchant from Kemper County. Together, Ragsdale and Ball, who would later be recognized as the city's founders, began subdividing their respective land holdings into lots to facilitate new development.

The settlement's naming sparked intense debate among its residents. The industrially-minded faction, led by Ball, advocated for "Meridian," interpreting it as equivalent to "junction." Meanwhile, farming-oriented settlers preferred "<unk>," derived from a local creek's name and translating to "mad river" in Native American terminology. Ragsdale put forward his own suggestion: "Ragsdale City." Ball's railroad station on the Mobile and Ohio line displayed alternating signs - "Meridian" one day, "<unk>" the next. The matter was ultimately settled by the growing population of railroad workers, who favored "Meridian" and ensured it became the permanent name on the station. The settlement was formally incorporated as Meridian on February 10, 1860.

Meridian began as a modest village when the Civil War erupted in 1861. Its location at a crucial railroad intersection prompted the Confederacy to establish multiple military facilities to aid their war effort. In 1864, during the Battle of Meridian, Union General William Tecumseh Sherman led an assault on the city, systematically destroying railroad infrastructure in all directions, along with a weapons arsenal and extensive supply warehouses. Much of the city's structures were burned during this campaign. Sherman famously declared afterward, "Meridian, with its depots, store-houses, arsenal, hospitals, offices, hotels, and cantonments no longer exists." However, showing remarkable resilience, the city's railroad infrastructure was swiftly rebuilt, becoming operational just 26 days after the battle. The post-war Reconstruction period was marked by racial tensions, exemplified by the 1871 riot that occurred following a fire that devastated numerous businesses.

Following the Civil War, the town experienced significant growth, with its peak "Golden Age" occurring between 1880 and 1910. The development of railroad networks facilitated transportation and attracted various industries, triggering substantial population growth. This demographic expansion led to increased commercial activity in the downtown district. Meridian held the distinction of being Mississippi's largest city from 1890 to 1930, establishing itself as a prominent Southern manufacturing hub. This prosperous period left an architectural legacy, with numerous historic structures being erected during and shortly after this time, including the 1890 Grand Opera House, the 1894 Wechsler School, two Carnegie libraries constructed in 1913, and the city's tallest skyscraper, the <unk> Building, completed in 1929.

The city experienced sustained growth, driven by the commission government's successful initiative to attract 90 new industrial facilities in 1913 and the flourishing automotive sector during the 1920s. Despite the 1929 Wall Street crash and subsequent Great Depression, the city maintained its ability to draw new enterprises. As the Depression deepened and people sought diversions from daily hardships, downtown Meridian welcomed the S. H. Kress & Co. establishment, designed to "bring luxury to everyday citizens," alongside the Temple Theater, which served as a cinema. In 1933, the federal courthouse was constructed as part of the Works Progress Administration (WPA) program.

During a short economic lull following the Depression, America's involvement in World War II revitalized the railroad industry. Meridian regained its status as the area's railway hub, playing a crucial role in moving fuel and salvaged metal needed for military equipment production. This economic resurgence lasted until the 1950s, when personal cars and the new Interstate Highway System overshadowed train travel. As the railway sector deteriorated, many jobs disappeared, prompting residents to migrate elsewhere in search of employment.

During the 1960s Civil Rights Movement, Meridian served as a hub for civil rights activism, hosting a Council of Federated Organizations (COFO) office among other activist groups. Local resident James Chaney collaborated with Northern volunteers Michael Schwerner, his wife Rita, and Andrew Goodman to establish a community center. There, they conducted classes aimed at empowering African Americans to reclaim their voting rights. This activism faced strong opposition from local white residents, frequently leading to violent confrontations. In June 1964, Chaney, Schwerner, and Goodman traveled to Neshoba County, Mississippi, to investigate a recently bombed and burned black church. While returning to Meridian that night, the three men vanished. After an extensive FBI search, their bodies were discovered two months later, murdered and concealed in an earthen dam.

In a landmark verdict at Meridian's federal courthouse, seven members of the Ku Klux Klan, one of whom was a deputy sheriff, were found guilty of civil rights violations in the Mississippi civil rights workers murders case, while three others were cleared of charges. This marked a historic moment as it was the first instance where a white jury had found a white law enforcement official guilty in a civil rights-related killing. The case saw new developments in 2005 when Mississippi state authorities reopened it and filed state charges for the first time, resulting in Edgar Ray Killen's conviction for manslaughter and subsequent 60-year prison sentence. To commemorate James Chaney, the city of Meridian renamed a section of 49th Avenue in his honor and established a yearly memorial service.

During the 1960s, following the development of new highway systems that improved commuting options, the downtown area experienced population decline as residents relocated to newly built subdivisions in the northern part of the city. In response to the influx of strip mall businesses moving into the downtown area, city officials took action in the 1970s and 1980s by establishing multiple historic districts to maintain the city's architectural heritage. This preservation effort led to two significant developments: the establishment of the Meridian Historic Districts and Landmarks Commission in 1979, followed by the launch of the Meridian Main Street program in 1985.

Meridian Main Street spearheaded various downtown revival initiatives, with a centerpiece project being the 1997 construction of a new Amtrak Station that replicated the city's demolished historic Golden Age station. The organization also undertook the restoration of several landmark buildings, including the 2001 Rosenbaum Building renovation and the 2002 rehabilitation of Weidmann's Restaurant, while promoting cohesive urban planning. In 2006, Meridian Main Street collaborated with The Riley Foundation to transform the historic Grand Opera House into the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and the Performing Arts."

After the Alliance for Downtown Meridian acquired control of Meridian Main Street in late 2007, these two entities, together with the Meridian Downtown Association, led the initiative to revitalize the downtown area. Acting as an umbrella organization, the Alliance provides administrative support and office space to the other two organizations while functioning as an intermediary between them. Although there were initiatives to restore the <unk> Building, these were terminated in early 2010 by newly elected Mayor Cheri Barry. Currently, the Alliance continues to champion downtown development and preservation, focusing particularly on attracting specialty shops, restaurants, and bars to create a more vibrant atmosphere both during daytime and evening hours. While the Meridian Downtown Association concentrates on increasing pedestrian activity through event organization, the Meridian Main Street program provides support to existing downtown businesses.

As a major railroad intersection, Meridian's steady flow of travelers spurred significant hotel development. Several prominent establishments, such as the Great Southern and Grand Avenue hotels, were established in the late 1800s, even before the city's peak prosperity period. The railroad industry's expansion and the 1906 construction of the original Union Station catalyzed further hotel construction to accommodate both passengers and railway employees. This building boom included the Elmira Hotel (1905), Hotel Meridian (1907), Union Hotel (1908), and Terminal Hotel (1910). The Union Hotel later gained recognition on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, while both Hotel Meridian and Grand Avenue Hotel were designated as contributing properties within the Meridian Urban Center Historic District.

The city's economic prosperity was mirrored in its architectural development, exemplified by the construction of the eleven-story Lamar Hotel skyscraper in 1927. The building, which was recognized on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, was later converted into a county annex facility. The structure received additional recognition in 1988 when it was designated as a Mississippi Landmark.

The E.F. Young Hotel, constructed in 1931, was a cornerstone establishment in the African-American commercial area that emerged on the western edge of downtown. During the segregation era, the establishment stood as one of the few places in the city where African-American travelers could secure lodging.

As suburban expansion flourished during the 1960s and 1970s, hotels largely relocated from the city center to outlying areas. Since 1985, Meridian has been governed by a mayor-council system, also known as a "strong mayor" structure. The city's demographic evolution has been shaped by various socioeconomic forces. From its establishment until 1970, each census showed population growth, with rates fluctuating dramatically from 165% to as little as 0.2%. The city experienced a significant 14% population reduction between 1980 and 2000. According to the 2000 census, the population stood at 39,968, with a population density of 885.9 residents per square mile (342.0/km2). By 2008, it ranked as the state's sixth-largest city, and census data from 2010 indicated further population growth.

Meridian serves as the main city of the Meridian metropolitan area, which encompassed three counties as of 2009: Clarke, Kemper, and Lauderdale, with a total population of 106,139. The surrounding region contains 232,900 people within a 45-mile (72 km) radius and 526,500 people within a 65-mile (105 km) radius.

While the city's total population has fluctuated over time, the non-white population has shown consistent growth in both absolute numbers and percentage. According to the 2010 Census, the city's demographic composition consisted of 61.55% African American residents, 35.71% White residents, 0.9% Asian residents, 0.2% Native American residents, less than 0.02% Pacific Islander residents, 0.59% residents of other racial backgrounds, and 0.89% residents identifying with two or more races. Additionally, Hispanic or Latino residents of any race constituted 1.75% of the total population.

Based on the 2000 Census data, Meridian had 17,890 housing units within its city boundaries, with 15,966 being occupied, including 10,033 family households. Among occupied homes, 31.1% included children under 18, while 36.2% housed married couples living together. Single-female households without a husband present made up 23.3%, and non-family households constituted 37.2%. Individual households represented 33.2% of the total, with 14.0% being seniors aged 65 or older living alone. Households averaged 2.39 persons, while families averaged 3.06 members. There has been a notable decline in average household size from 3.04 in 1970. The city's median age showed an upward trend, rising from 30.4 in 1970 to 34.6 in 2000.

The typical household in the city earned $25,085 annually, while the median family income stood at $31,062. Men in the workforce earned substantially more than women, with median incomes of $29,404 and $19,702 respectively. Individual residents averaged $15,255 in per capita income. Poverty affected a significant portion of the population, with 24.6% of families and 28.6% of all residents living below the poverty line. The impact was particularly severe among young people, as 40.8% of those under 18 lived in poverty, while 22.0% of seniors aged 65 and older also fell below this threshold.

The Meridian area demonstrates strong religious engagement, with religious affiliation in Lauderdale County reaching 65.2%, significantly higher than the national rate of 50.2%. Among those affiliated with religious organizations in 2000, the Southern Baptist Convention claimed the largest share at 30,068 members (59.0%), followed by the United Methodist Church with 9,469 adherents (18.6%), while the Catholic Church accounted for 1,872 individuals (3.7%).

German and Eastern European Jewish immigrants played a vital role in shaping the city's commercial growth through their establishment of various businesses and services. The founding of Congregation Beth Israel in 1868 preceded what would become the city's "Golden Age." At its peak in 1927, Meridian boasted Mississippi's largest Jewish population, with 575 residents of Jewish faith. Currently, the Jewish presence in Meridian has diminished significantly, with fewer than 40 residents, predominantly senior citizens.

Situated in Lauderdale County within Mississippi's North Central Hills region, Meridian encompasses a total area of 45.9 square miles (119 km²), as reported by the United States Census Bureau. This area comprises 45.1 square miles (117 km²) of land and 0.8 square miles (2.1 km²) of water. The city's strategic location places it 93 miles (150 km) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 km) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 km) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; 231 miles (372 km) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee; and 297 miles (478 km) west of Atlanta, Georgia. The surrounding landscape features a mix of cotton and corn fields interspersed with oak and pine forests, while the terrain is characterized by clay hills and lowlands formed by the headwaters of the Chickasawhay River.

The city's urban core has seen its natural landscape altered through grading, though the surrounding areas retain their gently undulating topography. The city is interlaced with various small creeks, while its northern and southern regions feature small lakes and wooded areas. The southern section is traversed by <unk> Creek, which splits to form Gallagher's Creek flowing through the city's center. In the far western section, Loper's Creek makes its course, while other minor waterways, including Shearer's Branch, Magnolia Creek, and Robbins Creek, are scattered throughout the city's expanse.

Located in the humid subtropical climate zone, Meridian experiences distinct seasonal temperatures. Summer months (June to August) typically see average highs of 90°F (32°C) and lows of 70°F (21°C). Winter temperatures (December to February) generally range from highs of 60°F (16°C) to lows of 35°F (2°C). July stands as the hottest month, reaching average highs of 92.9°F (33.8°C), while January records the lowest temperatures, with average lows dropping to 34.7°F (1.5°C).

The city receives an average yearly rainfall of 58.65 inches (1,490 mm), with precipitation distributed relatively uniformly throughout the year. March stands as the wettest month, recording an average rainfall of 6.93 inches (176 mm). Thunderstorms are responsible for much of this precipitation, occurring most frequently in summer but present year-round. The region experiences severe thunderstorms that can bring dangerous conditions including damaging winds, large hail, lightning strikes, and heavy rainfall. These intense weather events are most prevalent during spring, with a secondary peak in autumn, and they also pose the potential threat of tornadoes.

In its early days, railroads played a vital role in the city's economic foundation. By the beginning of the 1900s, it had become Mississippi's largest city, featuring five major railway lines and accommodating 44 daily train arrivals and departures. The city's prosperity stemmed not only from the railways themselves but also from the rail-transported commodities like timber and cotton. These railroad-centered industries established the city as a dominant economic force in both the state and region between approximately 1890 and 1930. When the railroad industry declined in the 1950s, the city's economy initially suffered but successfully transformed itself. Moving away from its railroad-dependent past, it developed a more diverse economic base, with the healthcare, military, and manufacturing sectors now serving as the primary employers.

Meridian, along with the city of Marion and Lauderdale County, receives support from the East Mississippi Business Development Corporation, established in 1996 through local business leaders' initiative. Despite the city's relatively modest civilian workforce of 15,420 as of April 2010, it draws from a substantial regional population: 232,900 people within a 45-mile (72 km) radius and 526,500 within a 65-mile (105 km) radius, with respective labor forces of 104,600 and 234,200. This positions Meridian as a central destination for employment, shopping, healthcare services, and cultural activities. The area maintains strong local employment, with 80% of Lauderdale County's workforce living within the county, and 90% residing within a 45-mile distance.

As of April 2010, Lauderdale County's healthcare sector employed 6,260 individuals. The region's dominant healthcare employer is Rush Hospital with 2,610 employees, while East Mississippi State Hospital and Anderson Hospital follow with 1,500 and 1,475 employees respectively. Meridian hosts three hospitals and numerous healthcare facilities. Jeff Anderson Regional Medical Center specializes in cardiovascular procedures, features a Level II NICU, and maintains a health and fitness facility. Rush Foundation Hospital, along with Rush Health Systems, manages the Specialty Hospital of Meridian, providing extended hospital care for patients requiring longer recovery periods. Riley Hospital specializes in stroke treatment and rehabilitation through its two dedicated centers. The healthcare landscape in Meridian also includes the Alliance Health Center and the historic East Mississippi State Hospital, which has served the community since 1882.

Retail serves as a significant source of employment in the county, providing jobs to 5,280 individuals as of April 2010. The city generates approximately $2 billion in annual retail sales. The Bonita Lakes Mall, spanning 633,685 square feet (58,871 m2), houses more than a hundred retail establishments, including department stores, specialty boutiques, restaurants, food outlets, and United Artists Theatres. The retail landscape expanded further with the completion of Meridian Crossroads' Phase I in November 2007, adding 375,000 square feet (34,800 m2) of shopping space in the Bonita Lakes area. Additionally, the North Hills Street shopping district has seen continuous growth, with new retail and office developments launched near the Highway 19 Walmart Supercenter in March 2007.

The region is supported by two key military installations: Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, which together provide employment for more than 4,000 area residents. NAS Meridian serves as a training facility for naval carrier pilots and other service members, and hosts the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy (RCTA), which delivers narcotics enforcement training to law enforcement personnel across the southeastern United States. The city, home to the state's first local Department of Homeland Security, leads both a nine-county regional response team and a twenty-nine county regional response task force. Key Field gained historical significance through the record-breaking endurance flight of brothers Fred and Al Key in 1935. Today, it hosts the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard and provides support facilities for the Army National Guard's 185th Aviation Brigade. The location also features an aviation history exhibit and houses Meridian's Aviation Museum.
