The area's notable businesses include Peavey Electronics Corporation, which has been producing guitars, amplifiers, and sound equipment from its headquarters in the city since 1965. The local industrial landscape also features companies such as Avery Dennison, Structural Steel Services, Sara Lee, Tower Automotive, and another corporation. Additionally, the city hosts four industrial parks.

The MSU Riley Center serves as a significant economic driver in downtown, generating income through tourism, cultural events, and entertainment. Each year, over 60,000 visitors are drawn to downtown Meridian by the Riley Center for various gatherings, conferences, and shows. A historic fixture on Front Street, Loeb's Department Store stands as a Mississippi retail institution, continuing its legacy through four generations of family ownership. Since its establishment by Alex Loeb in 1887, the store has maintained its reputation as a premier destination for quality men's and women's apparel.

Meridian's rich artistic heritage spans over a hundred years, with numerous cultural institutions and events shaping the city's creative landscape. The Meridian Art League, established in February 1933, marked one of the city's earliest artistic ventures. Initially hosting exhibitions at the downtown Lamar Hotel, the organization underwent a transformation in 1949, becoming the Meridian Art Association and diversifying its exhibition venues throughout the city. Following the closure of the Carnegie library located at 25th Ave and 7th St, the Art Association transformed the building into the Meridian Museum of Art, creating a permanent exhibition space. Since its 1970 opening, the museum has flourished, offering rotating exhibitions and comprehensive educational programs for visitors of all ages. The facility now presents more than thirty annual exhibitions, encompassing diverse mediums from traditional decorative arts and tribal artifacts to photography and crafts. Its permanent collection features notable works including 18th and 19th century portraiture, 20th century photography, and various sculptural pieces.

The Meridian Council for the Arts (MCA), established in 1978, serves as the official arts organization for both Meridian and Lauderdale County. The organization manages various programs including Community Art Grants, the annual Festival, workshops, and diverse special events throughout the year. MCA collaborates with numerous local arts institutions, such as the Meridian Museum of Art, Meridian Little Theatre, and Meridian Symphony Orchestra. The Meridian Little Theatre, established in 1932, stands as one of the oldest subscription-based community theaters in the South, attracting over 22,000 patrons each season and holding the distinction of being Mississippi's most popular community theatre. The Meridian Symphony Orchestra (MSO), which began in 1961, held its inaugural concert in 1962 and completed its first full season in 1963. A significant milestone was reached in 1965 when the MSO engaged its first international soloist, Elena Nikolaidi. The orchestra has contributed significantly to local music education by helping establish orchestra and strings programs in the Meridian Public School District and forming the Meridian Symphony Chorus. Under the leadership of Dr. Claire Fox Hillard, who has conducted since 1991, the orchestra planned to commemorate its 50th anniversary in February 2011 with a special performance by renowned violinist Itzhak Perlman.

The Grand Opera House, constructed in 1889 by half-siblings Israel Marks and Levi Rothenberg, was once a cultural landmark in the city. The venue's inaugural performance featured a German company's presentation of "The Gypsy Baron" by Johann Strauss II, and it went on to host numerous renowned artists and productions. The Great Depression forced its closure in the late 1920s, leaving the building deserted for approximately seven decades. In 2000, the Riley Foundation, established locally in 1998, provided a crucial $10 million grant for restoration, while additional funding of $15 million was secured through various city, county, and federal grants. The renovation concluded in September 2006, and the facility was renamed the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and Performing Arts." Today, the Riley Center features a 950-seat auditorium for live shows, a 200-seat studio theater, and 30,000 square feet (2,787 m²) of meeting facilities. The venue has become a major downtown attraction, drawing over 60,000 visitors annually for conferences, meetings, and cultural performances.

Meridian stands as an architectural gem, distinguished as one of the nation's best-preserved cities from the early 1900s. The city regularly attracts architecture students from across North America, who study its numerous buildings created by renowned architects. On Highland Park stands a unique distinction: the only Southern U.S. residence designed by Louis S. Curtiss, the Canadian-born architect celebrated for pioneering the glass curtain wall skyscraper. The city boasts the Frank Fort-designed Threefoot Building, widely regarded as one of America's finest Art Deco skyscrapers, drawing comparisons to Detroit's iconic Fisher Building. Notable California architect Wallace Neff left his mark on Meridian and the neighboring Alabama Black Belt region, taking commissions there during slow periods in California, thanks to his railroad executive relatives in Meridian and Selma. His work is particularly evident in the lower sections of Poplar Springs Drive, where his masterpiece at 2315 Poplar Springs Drive bears striking similarities to Falcon Lair, Rudolph Valentino's Benedict Canyon estate in Beverly Hills. While one Neff creation was demolished for Anderson Hospital's expansion in 1990 and another was lost to fire in Marion Park during the 1950s, his legacy endures. The Meridian Post Office showcases exceptional 1920s civic architecture, featuring bronze and Verde marble interiors, though its original art deco lighting fixtures were removed during 1960s renovations and now adorn private homes on Poplar Springs Drive and in North Hills.

Meridian has been designated as the site for the future Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center (MAEC). In 2001, the Mississippi Legislature endorsed the project, followed by a 2006 pledge of $4 million in matching funds contingent upon private donors raising $8 million. The city contributed $50,000 to the initiative in September 2007. The proposed MAEC would encompass 175 acres (71 ha) at Bonita Lakes, featuring an outdoor amphitheatre, an indoor concert venue, and a Hall of Fame celebrating Mississippi's artists. The Hall of Fame will be housed downtown in the former Montana's building, which, along with the neighboring Meridian Hotel building, was purchased for $300,000 in July 2010. The MAEC launched its Walk of Fame outside the Riley Center in February 2009 to generate interest in the planned Hall of Fame. Meridian native Jimmie Rodgers received the first star, followed by Mississippi blues legend B.B. King in September 2009. Literary giants Tennessee Williams, Eudora Welty, and William Faulkner were honored with stars on June 1, 2010, with actress Sela Ward joining them on June 24, 2010. The MAEC intends to expand the Walk of Fame with additional stars honoring Mississippi-born talents, including Morgan Freeman, Jimmy Buffett, Elvis Presley, Conway Twitty, and others.

The Temple Theater at the Shrine Temple serves as another major venue for large productions in the city. A notable feature is its 778-pipe Robert Morgan organ, representing one of only two Theater Organs in the state still in their original locations. During the silent film era, the Temple flourished with its impressive 1800-person capacity and boasted one of America's largest stages, surpassed only by New York City's Roxy Theater. Currently accommodating 1576 people, the Temple remains an active year-round venue, hosting various community events, theatrical performances, plays, musical concerts, Shrine organization activities, and special screenings of classic films.

Located in Highland Park, the Jimmie Rodgers Museum showcases "The Singing Brakeman's" original guitar alongside memorabilia chronicling his life and career, as well as steam-era railroad artifacts. The site features outdoor memorials and a historic steam locomotive in addition to the main museum structure. Meridian's significance as Rodgers' birthplace and his influence on Mississippi blues music is commemorated by a Mississippi Blues Trail marker, making it the first location outside the Mississippi Delta to receive this distinction. Additionally, on June 1, 2010, a Mississippi Country Music Trail marker was installed at Oak Grove Cemetery in Rodgers' honor. Since 1953, the city has maintained a tradition of hosting an annual festival in May to commemorate the anniversary of his passing.

Highland Park features a historic carousel built circa 1895 by Gustav Dentzel from Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Operating since 1909, the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel holds the distinction of being a National Historic Landmark and stands as the world's last remaining two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie. Its enclosure is unique as the only surviving original carousel building constructed using Dentzel's blueprints. The carousel's legacy inspired a community art initiative called "Around Town," which consists of 62 carousel horse sculptures. These pieces, sponsored by local residents and businesses and created by area artists, are displayed throughout the city and county.

The city features diverse recreational areas, with Highland Park, Bonita Lakes, and [Lake Name] being notable destinations. Highland Park provides year-round access to various amenities including picnic areas, swimming facilities, tennis courts, and fields for baseball and softball, along with a playground. Bonita Lakes, a municipal property spanning 3,300 acres (13 km2), encompasses three lakes and the Long Creek Reservoir. This expansive park features the Lakeview Municipal Golf Course and extensive recreational facilities, including nature and equestrian trails, walking and jogging tracks, cycling paths, pavilions, picnic spots, boating facilities, paddle boat rentals, food services, and fishing areas. The Bonita Lakes vicinity also houses major retail developments: Bonita Lakes Mall, Bonita Lakes Crossing, and Bonita Lakes Plaza. [Lake Name], a 7,150-acre (28.9 km2) facility, features a 4,144-acre (16.77 km2) lake offering diverse activities such as boating, fishing, swimming, water skiing, picnicking, hunting, hiking, and camping. The lake area also includes Splashdown Country Water Park, a 25-room motel, and cabin accommodations.

Since 1992, Meridian has served as the venue for the State Games of Mississippi, an annual Olympic-style multi-sport competition held across the state. The event operates under the National Congress of State Games, which maintains ties with the U.S. Olympic Committee. The inaugural games drew 1,200 athletes competing in twelve sports, and participation has grown significantly, with over 70,000 athletes having taken part since its inception. The 2009 edition featured more than 4,500 participants across 27 sporting disciplines. Athletes who compete in these games are eligible to participate in the Southeast Sports Festival, while those who earn medals qualify for the State Games of America, held every two years.

The State Games were initially a single-weekend event in June, but expanded to span two weekends as they incorporated more sports. The opening ceremonies consistently take place in downtown Meridian on June's third Friday. Multiple sports facilities across the city host the competitions, with key venues including Northeast Park and the Davidson Complex, among other fields. Northeast Park, situated along Highway 39, spans 85 acres (34 ha) and features comprehensive facilities: ten tennis courts, four softball fields, three soccer fields, an asphalt track, and a spacious picnic pavilion. The Davidson Sports Complex offers six tennis courts, four softball fields, and a half-mile track. Additional sporting venues include the Meridian Jaycee Soccer Complex, Sykes Park, and Phil Hardin Park.

The city features multiple golf courses, with Lakeview Municipal Golf Course being a notable public 18-hole facility that welcomes daily players. Located along Highway 39 North, Briarwood County Club is an exclusive establishment offering golf, swimming, fishing, and restaurant amenities. The city's golfing options are further complemented by several other facilities, including Northwood Country Club, Creek Golf Center, and Ponta Creek Golf Course.

The Crescent line operated by Amtrak provides rail service from Meridian to major East Coast cities including New York City, Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Washington, D.C., as well as southern destinations such as Charlotte, Atlanta, Birmingham, and New Orleans. Located at 1901 Front Street within the historically significant Meridian Downtown Historic District, the Union Station Multi-Modal Transportation Center serves as a central transit hub. The facility, which was initially constructed in 1906, demolished in 1966, and reconstructed in 1997, integrates multiple transportation services including the Meridian Transit System, Amtrak railways, Norfolk Southern rail corridor, and bus services from Greyhound, Trailways, and other transit operators. The combined annual passenger count across Amtrak trains, Greyhound buses, and Meridian Transit System buses reaches 242,360.

The Meridian Regional Airport, situated at Key Field on Airport Boulevard South, is located 3 miles (4.8 kilometers) southwest of the city. The airport features Mississippi's longest public runway, measuring 10,004 feet (3,049 meters). Operating since 1930, the facility provides daily air service connecting to Dallas/Fort Worth, Texas.

During the economic hardships of the Great Depression, the city's residents considered closing down the airport due to maintenance expenses. However, airport managers and siblings Fred and Al Key devised an innovative solution in 1935 to preserve the facility. Flying their aircraft, dubbed the "Ole Miss," the Key brothers remained airborne from June 4 to July 1, 1935, setting an extraordinary endurance record of 653 hours and 34 minutes. Their remarkable achievement generated sufficient media attention and financial support to ensure the airport's survival. The facility was subsequently named Key Field in honor of the brothers, whose conventional flight endurance record still stands today.

The foundation of public education in Meridian was established under the Mississippi Constitution of 1870. The Board of School Directors, whose members were appointed by the City Council, managed the school system from 1870 to 1885. Prior to 1884, education in the city was primarily provided by private institutions, which served only around 400 students. The city's first public school facility wasn't constructed until September 1884. African American students initially attended classes in rented space at St. Paul Methodist Church. A significant development occurred in January 1888 when the Mississippi Legislature modified the city charter, enabling Meridian to establish its own municipal school district. Shortly after, in March, voters approved a $30,000 bond measure for new school construction. This funding led to the construction of the Wechsler School in 1894, marking a historic milestone as the state's first brick public school building constructed for African American students.

The Meridian Public School District evolved from its initial area and subsequent expansions to reach its present-day scale, encompassing six elementary schools, three middle schools, and three high schools. Several private institutions also operate within the city, including Lamar School, Calvary Christian School, Community Christian School, and St. Patrick's Catholic School. Meridian High School, serving as the district's primary high school, spans 37 acres (15 ha) with six buildings containing 111 classrooms. The school serves grades 10-12 and has a student population of approximately 1,500.

Meridian hosts two institutions of higher education. Meridian Community College, established in 1937, is situated at 910 Highway 19 N and provides tuition-free education for four semesters to students graduating from Meridian Public and Lauderdale County School Districts, including local homeschooled students residing in Lauderdale County. The institution, initially called Meridian Junior College and based at Meridian High School, relocated to its current site in 1965. Following integration, it merged with the previously African-American T.J. Harris Junior College in 1970. The institution adopted its current name, Meridian Community College, in 1987 to "better represent the range of educational opportunities available to the expanding community." Mississippi State University also maintains a campus in Meridian. During the Fall 2008 term, the institution served 763 students from 33 Mississippi counties and several Alabama locations.

Meridian's current public library system, known as the Meridian-Lauderdale County Public Library, is situated at the intersection of 7th Street and 26th Avenue. The city's library history is notable for having two Carnegie libraries constructed in 1913, segregated for white and black communities. The initiative began in the 1880s when a women's group called the Fortnightly Book and Magazine Club started collecting books and fundraising for a city library. Their collection later formed the foundation of Meridian's library holdings. The group gained broad community support and enlisted local leader Israel Marks to seek funding from philanthropist Andrew Carnegie. The African American library, built on land donated by St. Paul Methodist Church at 13th Street and 28th Avenue, held the distinction of being both the state's only black library until after World War I and the nation's only Carnegie library specifically built for African Americans. The white library was established in a building previously owned by First Presbyterian Church members, who sold it to the city on September 25, 1911. These separate facilities operated until 1967, when integration mandated by the Civil Rights Act of 1964 led to the merger of their collections at the current location. The former white library was transformed into the Meridian Museum of Art in 1970, while the historic African-American library was ultimately demolished on May 28, 2008.

The Meridian Star, established in 1898, stands as the city's sole daily newspaper. Initially published as The Evening Star, it underwent a name change in 1915 and has remained the exclusive daily publication in Meridian since 1921. As of March 2010, the newspaper maintained a daily circulation of approximately 12,000, serving readers across Lauderdale County and neighboring areas in western Alabama and eastern Mississippi.

While the Meridian Star currently stands as the city's sole printed newspaper, several historical publications once served the community. Notable among these was the Memo Digest, a 1970s publication ranging from ten to twenty pages in length. Catering primarily to the African-American community, the Digest reached approximately 5,000 readers. The city's rich journalistic history also included various other newspapers: The Colored Messenger, The State, The Weekly Mercury, The Blade, Weekly Echo, Fair Play, The Meridian Morning Sun, Teacher and Preacher, and Clarion.

Meridian serves as the main city in its Designated Market Area (DMA), encompassing 72,180 television-equipped households. The local ABC affiliate broadcasts from 815 23rd Avenue and operates two digital subchannels: one affiliated with MyNetworkTV and another serving as Meridian's CW station. The NBC affiliate, based at 1151 Crestview Circle, has also carried FOX programming since January 5, 2009, along with content from the Retro Television Network (RTN). Through a program services agreement, it collaborates with the local CBS affiliate, which maintains a local service on its secondary subchannel. The area is also served by a Mississippi Public Broadcasting affiliate.

The city serves as the main hub of the Meridian Arbitron Radio Market, encompassing an audience of 64,500 listeners aged 12 and above. Based at Highway 45 North, the radio station at FM 105.7 dominated the market with a 14.8% share during Fall 2009. FM 104.1 followed in second place with 11.1% of listeners, while AM 1010 secured third position with 7.4%. The market features several other notable stations, including FM 97.9, FM 97.1, FM 106.9, AM 1450, and FM 95.1. Listeners can access Mississippi Public Broadcasting through FM 88.1.

The Meridian-born rapper Big K.R.I.T., signed to Island Def Jam, has established himself through numerous mixtapes and albums including K.R.I.T. Wuz Here and others. His growing fanbase appreciates both his lyrical prowess and self-produced instrumentals, along with his versatility in crafting diverse songs ranging from introspective, slower pieces like "The Vent" to energetic, dynamic tracks such as "Mt. Olympus."

Paul Davis, who achieved fame with his pop hits "I Go Crazy" and "'65 Love Affair" in the late 1970s and early 1980s, was born in Meridian in 1948. Following his retirement from his musical career, he chose to return to his hometown, where he lived until he passed away from a heart attack in 2008.

Chris [Last Name] (February 10, 1947 – April 23, 2012) was an American bass guitarist known for his work in country rock. He played with both the International Submarine Band (ISB) and The Flying Burrito Brothers, collaborating with Gram Parsons on several songwriting projects. Throughout his career, [Last Name] performed alongside numerous notable artists, including Jackson Browne, Judy Collins, Ry Cooder, Whitney Houston, Willie Nelson, Randy Newman, Linda Ronstadt, Leon Russell, Nancy Sinatra, Johnny Winter, and The Byrds.

The city has produced numerous notable athletes who have reached professional ranks in various sports. These include Major League Baseball pitchers Dennis "Oil Can" Boyd and Jay Powell, Negro league catcher Paul Hardy, professional basketball players Derrick [name] and George Wilson, and NFL player Joe Stringfellow.

Papa Stour, the eighth largest island in Scotland's Shetland archipelago, spans 828 hectares (3.2 square miles) and lies west of mainland Shetland. The island's current population, numbering fewer than twenty, includes settlers who arrived following a population recruitment initiative in the 1970s. The island's distinctive landscape features an impressive array of geological formations, carved by marine erosion of volcanic rock, including numerous caves, stacks, arches, blowholes, and cliffs. Rich in biodiversity, both the island and its surrounding waters support varied wildlife communities. The western portion of Papa Stour has been designated as a Site of Special Scientific Interest, while its encompassing waters are protected as a Special Area of Conservation.

The island features multiple burial chambers from the Neolithic period and contains ruins of a house from the 13th century belonging to Duke Hakon, dating to the Norse period of occupation. During the 1800s, the population grew to at least 380 people, coinciding with the establishment of a fishing station at West Voe. Though the population later experienced a continuous decrease, reaching as low as 16 residents in the 1970s, the numbers have since shown improvement.

Papa Stour sits at the southwestern edge of St Magnus Bay. The island features 34 kilometers (21 miles) of dramatic coastline, characterized by many small inlets and four major 'voes'. Hamna Voe (from Old Norse meaning 'harbor bay') in the south provides the most protected anchorage, with its surrounding cliffs featuring a natural arch formation. Housa Voe on the eastern side (from Old Norse meaning 'house bay'), though less protected, serves as the island's primary harbor and where the ferry docks.

Holm and Maiden Stack serve as natural guardians at the harbor's southern entrance. Holm, accessible during low tide, historically served as a colony for supposed lepers until the 1700s, though historical evidence suggests these individuals may have actually suffered from vitamin deficiency rather than leprosy. Maiden Stack derives its name from a 14th-century tale involving Lord Thorvald, who built a small dwelling (its remains still visible today) atop the stack to keep his daughter away from suitors. His plan proved futile, however, as she was later discovered to be with child; an alternative version of the tale recounts her successful elopement with a local fisherman. The northern coastline features West Voe, with its inner section known as 'Voe,' serving as the primary inlet, while the smaller Voe lies just to the west.

The island's principal settlement is <unk>, situated with views over <unk> Voe and encircled by cultivated land east of the hill dyke (extending southward from West Voe). A strip of glacial moraine, roughly one and a half kilometres long, divides the island's western portion. The majority of the remaining terrain features a shallow, rocky soil, likely originating from glacial deposits. The island is notable for its near-complete lack of peat deposits, and its volcanic bedrock contributes to relatively rich soil conditions. This peat scarcity historically led to residents removing turf for fuel, resulting in exposed rock surfaces throughout the interior.

Along the coastline of Papa Stour, numerous smaller islets and skerries complement the larger islands previously discussed. The coastal features include various formations such as Stack, multiple Skerries, Holm, and Stacks, along with specifically named locations like the Holm of Melby, Koda Skerry, Lyra Skerry, Sula Stack, Swat Skerry, The Horn, and Wilma Skerry. Located 5 kilometers (3.1 miles) northwest are the Ve Skerries, which comprise North Skerry, The Clubb, and several other formations. Between Papa Stour and the Ve Skerries extends the shallow bank known as Papa.

On June 21, 2008, the sole inhabitant and proprietor of a small island called <unk> Holm, Stuart Hill, proclaimed its independence by establishing the Crown Dependency of <unk>. Hill, who renamed the 1-hectare (2.5-acre) island to "<unk> Island," based his claim on a 1468 matrimonial agreement between Norway's King Christian and Scotland's King James III. Through this historical connection, he contended that the island should be classified as a British crown dependency, therefore existing outside both the United Kingdom and European Union. However, the UK government did not acknowledge this declaration.

The island's geological composition consists of volcanic and sedimentary formations dating back to the Devonian era, during which Scotland was situated approximately 10-25 degrees south of the equator as part of the Old Red Sandstone Continent. The Old Red Sandstone deposits, which accumulated between 408 and 370 million years ago, were formed when previously existing Silurian rocks were elevated during Pangaea's formation, subsequently eroded, and deposited in river deltas. Along the margins of the eroding mountains existed Lake Orcadie, a freshwater body extending from Shetland to the southern Moray Firth. Papa Stour's primary structure comprises volcanic materials from this period's volcanic activity, including solidified layers of volcanic ash and rhyolite lava, with a notable Devonian fish bed present at Lamba Banks. The landscape also features numerous large boulders left behind by glacial activity during the Pleistocene period.

The relentless action of the sea on the island's soft volcanic rock formations has sculpted a remarkable collection of geological features, including caves, sea stacks, natural arches, blowholes, steep cliffs, voes (narrow bays), and inlets that rank among Britain's most impressive. The 'Holl' cave formation penetrates completely through the island's northwestern tip, extending nearly half a mile and maintaining sufficient width for boat passage. In the southwestern region, another notable cave known as Christie's Hole suffered a partial roof collapse in 1981, creating a dramatic natural feature. Near the western voe lies 'Francie's Hole,' a cave that particularly captivated Victorian writer John Tudor, who documented his admiration for this formation in his personal memoirs.

Marine mammals including otters, grey seals, killer whales, and harbour porpoises are common visitors to the waters surrounding Papa Stour. The island serves as a breeding ground for various seabirds and shorebirds, such as Atlantic puffins, Arctic and common terns, Arctic skuas, northern fulmars, common guillemots, razorbills, curlews, wheatears, ringed plovers, and great black-backed gulls. Additionally, the island has documented numerous species of migratory birds.

The island boasts an abundance of wildflowers, with notable species such as mountain everlasting, spring squill and various others, alongside the widespread heather. The western portion of the island holds designation as a Site of Special Scientific Interest, while its surrounding waters are protected as a Special Area of Conservation. The iconic Shetland Pony continues to be raised here.

The island's human history began around 3000 BC, evidenced by surviving Neolithic tombs called 'heel-shaped cairns.' While information about the pre-Celtic and Celtic periods remains scarce, historical records suggest that when Norse settlers arrived, they discovered a religious community on the island. This is reflected in the island's name, which translates to "Big island of the Papar" (referring to Celtic monks), distinguishing it from Papa Little, situated approximately 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) westward.

A document from 1299, written in Old Norse, represents the oldest surviving text from Shetland and centers on Papa Stour. The manuscript recounts a dramatic event that occurred in the residence of Duke Hakon Magnusson, who would later ascend to become King Hakon V of Norway. Near the beach at Voe, one can find a stone circle, which marks the remnants of a 'ting' (a local assembly site). This location witnessed a duel involving Lord Thorvald, who emerged victorious despite facing accusations of corruption in the 1299 document and was subsequently known as 'dominus de.' (His daughter's tragic tale is mentioned earlier.) The thirteenth-century house that belonged to Duke Hakon can still be found in ruins near Voe.

Scotland gained nominal control of Shetland in 1469, though Norwegian nobles (known as 'Lairds of Norway') retained their estates on Papa Stour into the 1600s. German merchants from the cities of Bremen and Hamburg established a seasonal trading post in the 1500s to purchase fish from local fishermen. During the 1700s, the island came under the ownership of two Scottish landowners: Thomas Gifford of Busta and Arthur Nicolson of Lerwick. Under their leadership, they ran a successful deep-sea fishing operation (called 'haaf' in Old Norse), which operated during summer using traditional six-oared vessels called sixerns.

The church on the island, situated with a view over Kirk Sand in Fore Wick bay, was established in 1806. Approximately 300 meters away from the current church building, there are possible remains of an earlier chapel site on the headland between Kirk Sand's western edge and another bay. Local residents know this location as the 'old kirk,' and the Ordnance Survey documents it as a chapel site dating back to approximately the 12th century. According to local legend, supernatural forces repeatedly interfered with the construction at this original site, with each day's progress being mysteriously undone during nighttime hours. The story tells that these otherworldly entities eventually relocated the cornerstones to where the church stands today, and only then did construction proceed without incident. Archaeological investigations conducted in 2004 lent some credence to this oral tradition, revealing only large rhyolite blocks and a fragment of whale bone rib at the original site.

In the 19th century, West Voe became home to a new fishing station, and the island's population grew to exceed 360 residents. However, beginning in the 1870s, the population declined due to fuel scarcity and reduced fishing activity following the introduction of steam-powered drifting vessels. During this period, Papa Stour witnessed another notable duel-related incident. Edwin Lindsay, a military officer from the Indian army and son of the 6th Earl of Balcarres, was deemed mentally unstable and exiled to the island after declining to participate in a duel. He remained imprisoned there for 26 years until 1835, when Quaker minister Catherine Watson secured his freedom. A spring in the southern part of the island, known as Lindsay's Well, marks the spot where he was permitted to take his baths.

Around Dutch Loch, there are notable examples of horizontal water mills, commonly referred to as Norse or Clack Mills. These structures were typically two stories high with roofs made of turf, and were strategically constructed into banks to provide access to the upper level where the millstone was located. The interior featured a stationary bottom millstone and an upper millstone that rotated, powered by water cascading onto paddles beneath. Several of these mills remained operational on Papa Stour into the early 1900s, and today, one functioning example can still be found on the Burn of Quendale, at Quendale in Shetland's south Mainland.

Like many other small Scottish islands, Papa Stour saw its highest population numbers in the 19th century, followed by a notable downward trend (similar to Mingulay). The population had dwindled to sixteen mostly elderly inhabitants by 1970, coinciding with the closure of the island's school. However, a turning point came through an Exchange and Mart advertisement offering newcomers a free croft and five sheep, which generated overwhelming interest. This initiative proved successful, with the population rising to 33 by 1981. The community's stability was later disrupted by internal conflicts that resulted in legal proceedings, causing the population to decrease to 20 by 2005 and leading to another school closure. A further decline occurred when a family of seven departed, leaving just nine residents by early 2008. The 2011 census documented 15 permanent residents, contrasting with the overall 4% growth seen across Scottish islands during 2001-2011, which reached a total of 103,702 inhabitants.

The fishing vessel Ben Doran from Aberdeen ran aground on the Ve Skerries, located 3 miles northwest of Papa Stour, during the evening of March 28, 1930, as she made her way to Scalloway to unload her catch. Though weather conditions were relatively favorable when the vessel struck the rocks, the wreck wasn't spotted and reported until the next day by a passing trawler. Despite rescue efforts mounted by coastguard personnel and local volunteers (as Shetland lacked a lifeboat station at the time), the weather had grown so severe that approaching the skerries became impossible. Although authorities requested assistance from the Stromness lifeboat in Orkney, 120 miles distant, the call for help came too late to make a difference. The disaster claimed all nine crew members, with only three bodies recovered: James Mitchell, whose remains were transported back to Aberdeen, and J. Cormack and J.R., who were laid to rest in Scalloway.

The SS Highcliffe, a cargo vessel, became stranded on the shores of Holm during foggy conditions in February 1940. Fortunately, due to favorable weather at the time, while the vessel and its contents were lost, there were no casualties. Later, in 1967, another incident occurred when the Juniper, a fishing trawler from Aberdeen, ran aground in Lyra Sound beneath towering 60-meter (200-foot) cliffs. The local lifeboat crew successfully rescued all 12 crew members, and their coxswain received the RNLI silver medal for his heroic efforts in the rescue operation.

The most recent shipwreck near Papa Stour took place on December 9, 1977, when the Aberdeen fishing vessel Elinor Viking, commanded by Captain Alec Flett, ran aground on the Ve Skerries. Though the local Lifeboat responded, severe sea conditions prevented it from approaching close enough to perform a rescue. Following a request from Lerwick's Coastguard Station Officer, Alec Webster, a British Airways Sikorsky helicopter crew volunteered and launched from Sumburgh Airport. Despite battling storm-force winds, they successfully winched the entire ship's crew to safety within hours of the vessel's grounding. The helicopter team was later decorated for their courageous actions. While everyone survived the incident, it served as the catalyst for two significant developments: the construction of a lighthouse on the skerries in 1979 and likely influenced the establishment of the current Search and Rescue helicopter unit at Sumburgh Airport.

Crofting remains central to life on the island. The agricultural economy primarily relies on sheep farming, though residents also raise various other livestock including cattle, pigs, goats, and various poultry such as chickens, ducks, and geese. Vegetables are cultivated in protected circular-walled gardens, locally known as 'scrubs'. While fishing continues, it operates at a modest scale. The island's infrastructure is basic, with just a post office near the pier and no retail stores. Modern amenities arrived late, with electrical grid connection only established in the late 1990s. The island hosts the Papa Stour Project, a Christian initiative providing housing support for men recovering from substance abuse. Transportation to the mainland is provided by ferries crossing the Sound of Papa to West Mainland Shetland, taking 45 minutes. Though the ferry accommodates vehicles, the island's road network is limited to a single short route. For visiting boats, the four main voes offer protected anchorage, though mariners must exercise caution due to strong tidal currents in both the Sound of Papa and the northwestern waters.

It serves as the "Father" figure in the poem "Da Sang o da Papa men," which has since become integrated into folk music tradition after being musically arranged by Manson. The recurring choral refrain, "Foula Doon!", creates a particularly memorable impact.

"Out of sight of Foula!" describes the fishermen's traditional practice of navigating their open boats until Foula's towering cliffs disappeared from view, positioning them approximately 96 kilometers (60 miles) west of Papa Stour. The phenomenon known as 'tide-lumps' describes unusually large wave formations created when wind and tide forces interact. The poem concludes with a powerful image of the fishermen finding their way back to Papa guided by the distinctive scent carried across the waters. This demonstrates the author's masterful ability to evoke sensory details that bring the scene to life. The poem takes on additional significance knowing that the Da Horn o Papa landmark crumbled during a storm around when the poem was written, making it both a commemoration of traditional fishing practices and a tribute to a lost geographical landmark.

"Angel of Death" serves as the first track on Reign in Blood, the 1986 album by American thrash metal band Slayer. Composed by Slayer's guitarist Jeff Hanneman, both musically and lyrically, the song focuses on Josef Mengele, the Nazi doctor who performed horrific human experimentation at Auschwitz concentration camp during World War II. The controversial subject matter resulted in persistent accusations of Nazi sympathy and racism against the band throughout their years in music.

The song "Angel of Death," though controversial and responsible for postponing Reign in Blood's release, has become a staple in Slayer's live performances, appearing on all their concert albums and video releases, as well as in multiple films. Critics have praised the track, with AllMusic reviewer Steve Huey notably designating it as a "classic."

Slayer's Jeff Hanneman composed "Angel of Death" after studying literature about Josef Mengele, the Nazi doctor, during the band's tour. "I picked up a couple of books about Mengele at one of our stops. I thought to myself, 'This must be absolutely horrific.' When we were ready to record, those details were fresh in my mind — that's what inspired the lyrics for 'Angel of Death.'"

The text describes Dr. Josef Mengele's medical atrocities conducted at Auschwitz concentration camp during World War II. His research primarily targeted twins and dwarfs, subjecting them to extensive physical and psychological tests. The song "Angel of Death" references several of his brutal procedures, including surgeries performed without anesthesia, blood transfusions between twins, isolation experiments, exposure to gas, injections of deadly pathogens, forced gender reassignment procedures, and the surgical removal of body parts and organs.

"'Together, joining heads. Just a matter of time 'til you rip yourselves apart,' a lyric from the second-to-last verse, references the reported experiments of Mengele involving twin surgeries. According to testimony from Auschwitz survivor Vera Alexander during the 1961 trial of Adolf Eichmann (known as the 'Holocaust's architect'), Mengele allegedly conducted horrific procedures where he surgically connected twins - specifically, attaching a deformed twin to their sibling back-to-back, including their wrists, and joining their blood vessels to create conjoined twins. This disturbing account gained broader public attention when Alexander appeared in the 1985 documentary 'The Search for Mengele,' and her testimony has since been cited by various scholars, including Mengele researcher Gerald Posner."

The controversial lyrics of "Angel of Death" played a significant role in delaying Slayer's 1986 album Reign in Blood. While the band was under contract with Def Jam Records, their distributor Columbia Records rejected the album's release, citing concerns over both its lyrical content and cover art, which they considered "excessively graphic." The album ultimately found distribution through Geffen Records and was released on October 7, 1986. Nevertheless, the contentious nature of the material led Geffen Records to exclude Reign in Blood from their official release calendar.
